header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Emerald CTO), Tom Reynolds (Emerald SRE Lead), Nina Gomez (Emerald Head of Platform)
summary: Discovery focused on reliability, incident tolerance, multi-region routing and fallback policies. Emerald is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for a customer-facing recommendation engine with strict uptime and data residency needs. Key asks: multi-region failover behavior, SLA guarantees, canary/rollout strategies, KV cache consistency across regions, and proof-of-concept benchmarking.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
Security and compliance (SOC2, KMS, audit logs)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:04] Aisha Patel: Yeah we can hear you, thanks Maya. I think we blocked about 40 minutes to go over reliability and failure modes related to Redwood deployment options.
[00:12] Carlos Ruiz: Great thanks, I'll jump in on the more technical bits. Quick agenda: current infra, traffic patterns, SLOs, what happens in incidents, and then we can go over fallbacks and recommendations. Sound good?
[00:20] Nina Gomez: Yep perfect.
[00:25] Tom Reynolds: Quick note, we have a tight timeline, want pilot by end of Q2, so any blockers on infra we'll need to flag earlier.
[00:31] Maya Chen: Got it, thanks Tom. Aisha, can you give a quick overview of what you're running today and the reliability expectations?
[00:40] Aisha Patel: Sure. We run a real-time recommendations API serving ~2k RPS peak for US, EU and APAC customers. Latency SLOs are 200ms p95 for the recommendation endpoint, availability target is 99.95% for customer-facing traffic. Some customers require data to stay in-region, so data residency matters. We currently have an in-house inference cluster for core models and use a managed provider for burst.
[01:05] Carlos Ruiz: Thanks. So primary concerns I hear: tight p95 latency, multi-region routing with residency, and clear failover behavior. A few questions from our side: do you expect active-active multi-region routing or active-passive for model serving?
[01:20] Tom Reynolds: Ideally active-active for latency, but for some EU accounts we want requests served from EU-only models. So we need policy-based routing by tenant.
[01:30] Maya Chen: That's doable; Redwood supports per-tenant routing policies. You can pin tenants to regions and set fallback policies that either fail closed or fail open to a different model/region depending on compliance rules.
[01:40] Nina Gomez: What's the behavior during an incident? Example: primary region has a control-plane outage but GPUs are still serving, or conversely, GPU pool is saturated.
[01:50] Carlos Ruiz: Good question. Typical Redwood fallback chain is: 1) local model variant in same region (quantized or smaller) 2) warm fallback to a dedicated model in another region (if policy allows) 3) last-resort hosted model in a neighboring region with auditing and customer notice. You can configure the policy per-route, per-tenant. In the control-plane outage case, if the data plane is unaffected we can keep serving; if the control plane blocks routing changes we rely on pre-provisioned runbooks and traffic policies.
[02:25] Aisha Patel: And that last point, pre-provisioned runbooks — do you have an example? We can't be reconfiguring things manually during an incident, need automated failover.
[02:34] Carlos Ruiz: Absolutely. We provide a declarative routing config that lives with your infra. You declare priorities and conditions: CPU/GPU utilization thresholds, latency barriers, error rate windows. Our controller can automatically shift traffic when thresholds are hit. We'll share a sample config.
[02:48] Tom Reynolds: How about KV cache consistency across regions? Our recommender uses a large KV cache for user session prefixes, losing that cache causes big tail-latency spikes.
[02:58] Carlos Ruiz: Right. For KV/cache we usually recommend local caches with a replication or warming strategy. Redwood supports prefix-based caching plus warm-starts on failover. The tradeoff is either slight cold-start latency on failover or paying for a globally replicated cache which increases cost.
[03:12] Nina Gomez: Do you support cross-region cache replication with eventual consistency? Our team can tolerate a small window where the cache isn't identical, but cannot tolerate stale PII across regions.
[03:22] Carlos Ruiz: Yes you can scope what goes into cross-region replication; sensitive data can be excluded. We also integrate with customer KMS so you can control encryption keys per-region.
[03:30] Aisha Patel: On SLA, you mentioned 99.95% is possible — is that for Dedicated only or Hosted too? What's the difference?
[03:38] Maya Chen: Short answer: Dedicated + Reserved capacity has the strongest SLA because you reserve GPU pools and get SLA-backed latency/uptime. Hosted can hit high availability but SLA tiers differ and we typically offer contractual SLAs for enterprise customers running dedicated or private deployments. We'll share the exact SLA language in the security pack.
[03:55] Tom Reynolds: If we start on Hosted to pilot and then move to Dedicated, what's the process and expected downtime for migration?
[04:03] Carlos Ruiz: We do blue-green style rollouts and can keep the same API layer. Typical migration is a config switch and model weights sync; downtime is minimal — mostly dependent on model size and weight transfer. We can do a warm-sync of model artifacts beforehand to minimize cutover.
[04:18] Maya Chen: Also note model variants and quantization profiles can be pre-provisioned in Dedicated to speed cutover.
[04:25] Aisha Patel: We have enterprise compliance requirements: SOC2, KMS integration, audit logs, SAML SSO, and we need encryption in transit and at rest. Also requirement for private deployment in some APAC accounts.
[04:36] Maya Chen: All supported. Private deployments meet the on-prem/VPC requirement; we can scope KMS/HSM integrations and provide audit log streams. We'll include the compliance artifacts in the pack.
[04:46] Tom Reynolds: For testing, we want to run a 100k requests benchmark with production-like traffic. Can Redwood run that or do we need to provide infra?
[04:55] Carlos Ruiz: We can help run benchmarks in a Redwood-managed staging environment or in your VPC for Private. For Dedicated we can provision a reserved pool for the window. We will need your traffic profile and sample prompts to make the test realistic.
[05:07] Aisha Patel: Regarding fallbacks — what do you do for function/tool-calls or streaming responses? If a fallback model has a different tokenization or behavior does Redwood normalize outputs?
[05:18] Carlos Ruiz: We do a best-effort normalization layer; streaming may fall back to chunked responses and we mark responses with metadata explaining fallback reason and model id. For tool-calls we keep a middleware layer to handle schema differences; we recommend smoke tests for endpoint compatibility.
[05:33] Maya Chen: Another point: cost. Active-active multi-region with replicated caches and pre-warmed pools will cost more. We can show cost tradeoffs and cost-control knobs like batching, quantization, and route-based model selection.
[05:46] Tom Reynolds: Yep cost is a big factor. We'll need to present a TCO for Dedicated vs Hosted for the pilot period.
[05:53] Maya Chen: We'll run a TCO delta analysis once we have traffic numbers.
[05:58] Nina Gomez: Quick question on observability — do we get per-request tracing and token-level cost breakdowns?
[06:05] Carlos Ruiz: Yes — Redwood Console exposes per-request traces, model-level latency breakdowns, and token-level cost estimators. You can also export traces to your existing observability stack.
[06:15] Aisha Patel: How do you handle rollback if a canary fails? Our policy is immediate rollback within 3 minutes if error rates exceed thresholds.
[06:24] Carlos Ruiz: Canary policies can be set with automatic rollback thresholds; we support rate-based and latency-based triggers. Rollback is automatic and you can configure notification hooks and runbooks.
[06:33] Tom Reynolds: Is there built-in chaos testing or support for injecting faults during the pilot?
[06:38] Carlos Ruiz: We don't ship chaos tooling but we integrate with existing chaos frameworks; we can help define failure injection scenarios and run them in the staging environment.
[06:47] Maya Chen: Ok I want to walk through a couple of scenarios — low-level outage and high-latency tail: First, region A network partition, region B unaffected. What's Emerald's desired behavior?
[06:57] Aisha Patel: For EU-bound traffic, we must fail closed (not send to non-EU) for regulated tenants. For general traffic we prefer failover to nearest region with degraded model if necessary.
[07:09] Carlos Ruiz: So config: per-tenant policy with a residency flag; default fallback route disabled for flagged tenants, enabled for others. Degraded model could be smaller quantized variant to preserve latency.
[07:20] Nina Gomez: How long does KV cache warm-up take when failing over? Any heuristics?
[07:26] Carlos Ruiz: Depends on model and cache size. Warm-up can take from seconds to a few minutes. We have strategies: pre-warm via background replication, prioritize most recent prefixes, or serve with degraded accuracy until warmed.
[07:38] Tom Reynolds: We can't accept multi-minute cold starts for top-tier customers.
[07:42] Carlos Ruiz: Understood. For those customers we recommend active-active with replicated warm caches or keep a hot-warm standby in the region which is more expensive.
[07:52] Aisha Patel: Can Redwood wave traffic gradually to fallback to reduce cold-start spikes?
[07:58] Carlos Ruiz: Yes — progressive shifting (10%, 30%, 60%) with circuit-breakers and latency windows. That's our typical canary-to-fallback flow.
[08:08] Maya Chen: Any concerns from your side on security for cross-region replication?
[08:12] Tom Reynolds: Just that PII must never leave the region for flagged tenants.
[08:16] Carlos Ruiz: We support field-level filtering so you can keep PII in-region. Also provide audit trails showing which keys/fields were replicated.
[08:26] Nina Gomez: For Private deployment, what's the visibility and how are upgrades handled?
[08:30] Maya Chen: Private deployment provides the same console and API but the control plane can be customer-managed. Upgrades are scheduled; you can do canary upgrades inside your control plane and Redwood provides the images and migration docs.
[08:41] Aisha Patel: For Dedicated, how do you guarantee capacity on spikes? We saw last holiday a 3x spike.
[08:49] Carlos Ruiz: Dedicated supports burst capacity options and autoscaling policies. You can reserve base capacity and allow short window burst using shared pools or cloud bursting; pricing differs.
[08:58] Tom Reynolds: Who handles incident comms if Redwood-managed? We need an integration into our PagerDuty and status page.
[09:04] Maya Chen: We integrate with PagerDuty, Slack, and have an incident status API. For enterprise SLAs we provide a named escalation path.
[09:12] Aisha Patel: Ok this is helpful. Let's talk about the pilot scope: we want a single route for US recommendations on Hosted, a reserved dedicated pool for EU compliance tenants in EU (maybe Dedicated or Private), and a fallback policy that never routes EU-regulated traffic outside EU. We'll test failover for US route to an adjacent region.
[09:30] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Proposed pilot: 2 weeks smoke in staging, 1-week load test (100k), then a limited production canary (5-10% traffic) for 2 weeks. We'll produce a runbook and config.
[09:42] Tom Reynolds: Timeline aligns with our Q2 target.
[09:45] Carlos Ruiz: I'll draft the routing/fallback examples and a sample config with thresholds and share it. Also add a checklist for cache warm-ups.
[09:55] Maya Chen: I'll send the security pack including SOC2, encryption, KMS details. Also I'll include the SLA language for Dedicated and Private.
[10:03] Nina Gomez: Any pricing markers we should expect for Dedicated with hot-warm standby per region? Ballpark is fine.
[10:08] Maya Chen: Ballpark: Dedicated base pool for one region with hot-warm standby could be 2-3x the base cost depending on GPU types and replication. We'll do a TCO once you share traffic.
[10:18] Aisha Patel: Competitors question — we currently evaluated Anthropic and considered self-hosted Triton for some internal models. How is Redwood different for our use case?
[10:27] Maya Chen: Redwood focuses on production serving ergonomics: unified runtime across Hosted/Dedicated/Private, routing policies out of the box, and observability for per-request costs. We also offer build/run guidance to avoid tail-latency pitfalls.
[10:39] Tom Reynolds: Ok. Couple of nitty gritty items: we use SAML SSO and have strict RBAC. Do you support SCIM for provisioning?
[10:46] Carlos Ruiz: Yes SCIM + SAML supported and we can map roles for least privilege.
[10:51] Aisha Patel: Good. Anything else from your side?
[10:55] Nina Gomez: No.
[10:57] Maya Chen: Great. Recap of next steps: I'll send security pack and SLA language; Carlos will share routing/fallback config and canary examples; Tom will share pilot traffic profile and spike windows. We'll sync on scheduling the 100k request benchmark.
[11:12] Tom Reynolds: Sounds good, thanks.
[11:15] Aisha Patel: Thanks everyone.
[11:18] Maya Chen: Thanks all, chat later.
